items.title: Assessing the Performance of AI Models in Misinformation Detection Using Predefined Social Noise Constructs
items.raw_content:
Authors: Manar Alsaid

Social media platforms generate vast volumes of user-generated content that often obscure meaningful discourse, a phenomenon conceptualized as social noise. While existing misinformation detection methods primarily focus on factual verification, they largely overlook the role of social noise in amplifying misinformation. This study assesses the performance of six text-based models and a graph neural network (GNN) in mitigating the effects of misinformation using predefined social noise constructs. The dataset consists of 500,000 tweets collected from the X platform using the Ukraine hashtag during the Russia-Ukraine conflict from March 2024 to March 2025. Advanced machine learning models achieve strong performance, with accuracies ranging from 79.94% to 97.17%. RoBERTa demonstrates the highest performance, with an accuracy of 97.17%, Cohen's kappa of 0.9660, MCC of 0.9660, and AUC of 0.9977. The GNN achieves an accuracy of 64.52% and an AUC of 0.899, demonstrating performance above random-chance classification by exploiting the relational structure between tweets. All text-based models achieve kappa values greater than 0.75, indicating substantial overall agreement. Explainable AI analysis using LIME reveals that 89.6% of predictive weight is attributed to contextual features rather than isolated keywords. The findings highlight that integrating social noise into AI pipelines enhances misinformation detection and supports more effective mitigation strategies in large-scale social media environments.
items.title_zh: 基于预定义社会噪声构念评估 AI 模型的虚假信息检测性能
items.summary: A study evaluates six text-based models and a graph neural network on 500,000 Ukraine-related tweets, with accuracies ranging from 79.94% to 97.17% and RoBERTa performing best at 97.17%. A LIME-based explainability check found that contextual features carried 89.6% of the predictive weight rather than isolated keywords.

items.title: REA: From Correct LLM Judgments to Safe Decision Delivery
items.raw_content:
Authors: Jingxiang Meng, Aofan Liu, Yaoshuai Ma, Fangxin Liu, Yongbiao Chen

Generative safety guards must classify requests correctly and return outputs that applications can parse. Reasoning guards can improve classification accuracy while producing outputs that applications cannot parse. When applications cannot extract a correct prediction, fallback handling can allow harmful requests or block safe ones. We introduce Resolve--Express--Act (REA), a framework that traces judgments through parsing and fallback to application actions. Experiments on classifiers and safety guards show that correct predictions can appear in incorrectly formatted outputs. Parsing the safety verdict preserves the reasoning guard's accuracy advantage, while stricter explanation requirements reject additional correct predictions. Accepting formatting variations recovers most rejected correct predictions. Held-out tests confirm that output requirements and generation limits affect whether correct predictions can be parsed. In our fail-open replay, matching the parser to the output and fixing formatting reduced the fraction of harmful requests allowed despite correct guard judgments from 95.5% to 0%. A fixed-output comparison shows that model-based extraction can preserve guard verdicts, but is not automatically reliable; deterministic normalization already repairs the observed native-format failures. Fallback replay shows that the same correct prediction can lead to different safety actions depending on the parser and fallback policy, including allowing requests the guard correctly identifies as harmful.
items.title_zh: REA：从正确的 LLM 判断到安全的决策交付
items.summary: The paper presents Resolve--Express--Act (REA), a framework for following safety-guard judgments through parsing and fallback decisions to the actions an application ultimately takes. In one fail-open replay, aligning the parser with the output format and correcting formatting cut the proportion of harmful requests that were allowed even though the guard had judged them correctly, from 95.5% to 0%.

items.title: Structure-preserving fidelity diagnostics for partial differential equations
items.raw_content:
Authors: Kyriakos Flouris

Machine learning surrogates of partial differential equations (PDEs) are commonly trained on data generated by numerical solvers. Therefore, the training data obey not the PDE but the modified equation of the numerical scheme, and the test loss, computed on data from the same solver, cannot distinguish a model that learned the physics from one that learned the discretization error. Here, we show that the difference is nevertheless visible in the trained model. We propose a suite of structure-preserving fidelity diagnostics, simple scores that measure whether a learned model respects one known property of the physics, such as a conserved quantity, a symmetry or a Hamiltonian structure, without access to the training data or the governing equation. Over five systems, the diagnostics track the error with respect to the true dynamics with a rank correlation of up to $0.94$, while the test loss is uncorrelated or anti-correlated with it. For the Burgers, Korteweg-de Vries and Navier-Stokes equations, the diagnostics separate numerical schemes that the test loss ranks as equivalent, including schemes of the same order. order.
items.title_zh: 偏微分方程的结构保持保真度诊断
items.summary: The paper proposes structure-preserving fidelity diagnostics that test whether a learned PDE surrogate honors known physics — conserved quantities, symmetries or Hamiltonian structure — without needing the training data or the governing equation. In tests over five systems, the scores followed the true-dynamics error with a rank correlation as high as 0.94, whereas test loss was uncorrelated or inversely correlated with it.

items.title: Efficient Fréchet Distributional Decoder Alignment for Latent Generative Models
items.raw_content:
Authors: Xianghong Fang, Jiajun Zhu, Esma Aimeur, Dehan Kong, Tim G. J. Rudner

Fréchet Distributional (FD) objectives provide an effective distribution-level signal for post-training generative models. For latent generative models, however, existing FD-based post-training methods optimize only the latent generator while keeping the decoder frozen: the decoder is trained on reconstruction latents obtained from real images but deployed on generator-produced latents at generation time. When these latent distributions differ, this \textbf{decoder train-generation mismatch} means that the decoder is deployed on inputs drawn from a distribution it was not directly trained on. We introduce \textbf{Fréchet Distributional Decoder Alignment (FDDA)}, an efficient post-training method that freezes the latent generator and directly optimizes the decoder on generation-time latents using an FD objective. A single epoch of FDDA consistently improves gFID and gFDr$^6$ across diverse flow-based and autoregressive latent generative models. Across all 11 evaluated models, FDDA reduces gFDr$^6$ by 34.0-59.6\% from the original pretrained models and provides a further 10.2-57.2\% reduction after generator-side FD post-training. FDDA also reduces total wall-clock time by factors of $3.6\times$-$328.7\times$ relative to generator-side FD post-training across these models. These results show that generator-side post-training alone does not exhaust the benefits of FD optimization, and that further gains can be obtained by adapting the decoder at substantially lower cost.
items.title_zh: 面向潜变量生成模型的高效 Fréchet 分布解码器对齐
items.summary: The paper proposes Fréchet Distributional Decoder Alignment (FDDA), which leaves the latent generator frozen and post-trains the decoder on latents produced at generation time with a Fréchet distributional objective. Across 11 models, FDDA reduced gFDr^6 by 34.0–59.6% and delivered a further 10.2–57.2% reduction after generator-side FD post-training, while cutting wall-clock time by 3.6× to 328.7× relative to generator-side post-training.

items.title: A Time-Synchronous Prequential Evaluation Framework for Next-Week Student Disengagement Prediction from Moodle LMS Logs
items.raw_content:
Authors: David Otoo-Arthur, Terence L. van Zyl

Retrospective evaluation of early-warning models may not reflect information available when predictions are issued and outcomes become observable. We developed a time-synchronous prequential framework for online prediction of next-week student disengagement, operationalised as inactivity onset, from Moodle logs. Ordered by calendar time, models were updated only with available outcomes and remained unchanged for all predictions at each prediction cutoff; development, calibration and evaluation were chronologically separate. We compared stochastic gradient descent logistic regression (SGD-LR), online sequential extreme learning machine (OSELM) and echo state network (ESN) across predictive performance, fixed, frozen and rolling threshold policies, calendar-time variation and four behavioural feature sets. Held-out evaluation comprised 49,329 predictions with 37.68% inactivity-onset prevalence. Discrimination was similar (average precision 0.665-0.679; ROC-AUC 0.755-0.774). OSELM had the highest recall, SGD-LR the highest precision and specificity, and ESN the highest Matthews correlation coefficient and balanced accuracy. Lower thresholds increased recall and alert volume, whereas rolling adaptation did not improve MCC over frozen thresholds. Weekly performance and calibrated-probability distributions varied without sustained deterioration. During model selection, cumulative-and-temporal features achieved the highest individual-set AP, with modest gains from combining all feature groups. These findings indicate that streaming early-warning evaluation should consider calibration, threshold-dependent performance, alert burden and calendar-time variation alongside aggregate discrimination.
items.title_zh: 基于 Moodle LMS 日志的下一周学生投入度下降预测：时间同步序贯评估框架
items.summary: The authors build a time-synchronous prequential setup for online prediction of whether a student will disengage the following week, defined as the onset of inactivity, using Moodle logs. Across 49,329 held-out predictions, OSELM led on recall, SGD-LR on precision and specificity, and ESN on Matthews correlation coefficient and balanced accuracy.

items.title: Longitudinal Learner Participation Profiling in Online Learning: Heterogeneous Consensus Clustering under Unequal Observation Windows
items.raw_content:
Authors: David Otoo-Arthur, Terence L. van Zyl

Learning management system traces are clustered to identify participation profiles, but unequal observation windows may cause profiles to reflect duration rather than participation alone. Using 16,448 complete learner--course sequences from 4,599 learners across 152 courses at a South African public university, we evaluated eight participation measures. All remained related to observation-window length even when expressed as rates or shares. Course-grouped adjustment reduced these relationships. Five retained measures were evaluated using K-means, Gaussian mixtures, Ward agglomerative clustering and K-medoids, with standardised measures and principal-component summaries. Evidence supported a broad two-profile grouping and a more detailed adjusted four-profile consensus: Gradually declining, Early-concentrated, Cyclical variable and Sustained active. Profile membership accounted for 2.87% of the variation in duration in the primary consensus, versus 38.18% using original measures. Mean assignment support was 0.739; 8.35% of assignments fell below 0.50, with greatest uncertainty in Sustained active. Two week-by-week sequence analyses agreed strongly with each other but only modestly with the four-profile consensus, indicating that the profiles combined multiple aspects of participation rather than distinct sequence patterns. Profiling should therefore assess duration effects, compare clustering methods and participation summaries, and report assignment consistency.
items.title_zh: 在线学习中的纵向学习者参与度画像：不等观测窗口下的异质共识聚类
items.summary: Drawing on data from 152 courses at a South African public university — 16,448 learner–course sequences in all — the study evaluates eight participation measures across 4,599 learners and finds that all remain related to observation-window length. Profile membership explained 2.87% of the variation in duration under the adjusted four-profile consensus, compared with 38.18% using the original measures; mean assignment support was 0.739.
